## OLD MCQs

## Background and Epidemiology

**1. What is the reported incidence of chronic pancreatitis (CP) per 100,000 inhabitants?**

- 1 to 3 per 100,000
- **5 to 15 per 100,000**
- 20 to 30 per 100,000
- 50 to 75 per 100,000

*Explanation: The reported rates show an incidence of approximately 5 to 15 per 100,000 and prevalence of 40 to 120 per 100,000 inhabitants calculated on the basis of an estimated median survival time of 20 years.*

**2. What is the reported prevalence of chronic pancreatitis per 100,000 inhabitants?**

- 10 to 25 per 100,000
- 25 to 35 per 100,000
- **40 to 120 per 100,000**
- 150 to 200 per 100,000

*Explanation: The reported rates show an incidence of approximately 5 to 15 per 100,000 and prevalence of 40 to 120 per 100,000 inhabitants calculated on the basis of an estimated median survival time of 20 years.*

**3. What is the most common cause of chronic pancreatitis?**

- Hereditary factors
- **Chronic alcohol consumption**
- Autoimmune disease
- Gallstones

*Explanation: Etiology of CP includes chronic alcohol consumption as the most common cause with an increasing impact accounting for 70% of all CP cases.*

**4. What percentage of all chronic pancreatitis cases are attributed to alcohol consumption?**

- 40%
- 55%
- **70%**
- 85%

*Explanation: Chronic alcohol consumption accounts for 70% of all CP cases.*

**5. What is the threshold alcohol intake for developing chronic pancreatitis?**

- 30 g/day for more than 6 months
- 50 g/day for more than 9 months
- **70 g/day for more than 12 months**
- 100 g/day for more than 18 months

*Explanation: A persistent alcohol intake of 70 g/day for a duration of more than 12 months is the threshold for developing CP.*

**6. What proportion of chronic pancreatitis is estimated to be hereditary?**

- 5% to 10%
- 10% to 15%
- **20% to 30%**
- 40% to 50%

*Explanation: Today, the proportion of hereditary CP is estimated at 20% to 30% of all CP patients.*

**7. Which gene mutation is NOT typically associated with hereditary chronic pancreatitis?**

- PRSS1 (cationic trypsinogen)
- SPINK1 (serine protease inhibitor Kazal-type 1)
- **BRCA1**
- CFTR (cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator)

*Explanation: The underlying genetic mutations include mainly mutations in gene loci of cationic trypsinogen (PRSS1), serine protease inhibitor Kazal-type 1 (SPINK1), carboxypeptidase A1 (CPA1), as well as cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR), chymotrypsinogen C (CTRC), and carboxyesterlipase (CEL). BRCA1 is not mentioned.*

**8. What percentage of chronic pancreatitis cases are currently classified as "idiopathic" after exclusion of other risk factors?**

- 1% to 5%
- **Approximately 10%**
- 20% to 25%
- 30% to 40%

*Explanation: "Idiopathic" CP is only accepted as a terminology after exclusion of all other risk factors and may account for approximately 10% of all cases today.*

**9. Why is the term "tropical pancreatitis" falling into disuse?**

- It has been replaced by "alcoholic pancreatitis"
- **It is actually strongly associated with genetic mutations/polymorphisms**
- It only occurs in temperate countries
- It has been proven to be caused by infectious agents

*Explanation: The term "tropical CP" is now falling into disuse as it has become evident that an aggressive form of idiopathic CP reported from India and other tropical countries is actually strongly associated with genetic mutations/polymorphisms in multiple genes.*

**10. What percentage of chronic pancreatitis patients have autoimmune pancreatitis (AIP)?**

- 1% to 2%
- **5% to 6%**
- 10% to 15%
- 20% to 25%

*Explanation: Autoimmune pancreatitis (AIP) is found in approximately 5% to 6% of all CP patients.*

**11. When was autoimmune pancreatitis first described?**

- 1985
- **1995**
- 2005
- 2010

*Explanation: Autoimmune pancreatitis (AIP) was first described in 1995.*

**12. Which type of pancreatitis is considered a presumed systemic IgG4-related sclerosing disease?**

- Alcoholic pancreatitis
- Hereditary pancreatitis
- **Autoimmune pancreatitis**
- Tropical pancreatitis

*Explanation: As a presumed systemic IgG4-related sclerosing disease, AIP is addressed in different guidelines and recommendations than CP.*

**13. What is the primary functional impairment in chronic pancreatitis?**

- Endocrine function
- **Exocrine function**

**14. Which clinical symptom is NOT associated with exocrine failure in chronic pancreatitis?**

- Steatorrhea

- **Hyperglycemia**

*Explanation: The clinical symptoms of exocrine failure include steatorrhea, weight loss, and maldigestion with intolerance of fatty food and malabsorption with vitamin deficiency; endocrine failure leads to symptoms of diabetes mellitus.*

**15. What is the key feature and most important symptom in nearly all chronic pancreatitis patients?**

- **Pain**

*Explanation: In the 1950s, two procedures approaching the dilated pancreatic duct from the left side were described by Duval and Puestow and Gillesby.*

**68. What modification did Partington and Rochelle make to the drainage procedure in 1960?**

- Added pancreatic tail resection
- **Abandoned the tail resection and opened the pancreatic duct throughout the entire aspect of the gland**
- Introduced the Roux-en-Y reconstruction
- Added bile duct drainage

*Explanation: In 1960 this approach was modified by Partington and Rochelle, who abandoned the tail resection and opened the pancreatic duct throughout the entire aspect of the gland.*

**69. What is the minimum duct dilation required for a Partington-Rochelle procedure?**

- 3 mm
- 5 mm
- **7 mm**
- 10 mm

*Explanation: Today, these procedures are performed in patients showing diffuse enlargement of the pancreatic duct > 7 mm, no accompanying mass-forming fibrosis.*

**70. What is the surgical morbidity rate for the Partington-Rochelle procedure?**

- 10% to 15%
- **Less than 10%**
- 20% to 25%
- 30% to 35%

*Explanation: This procedure shows very low surgical morbidity (<10%) and mortality (<1%).*

**71. What is the surgical mortality rate for the Partington-Rochelle procedure?**

- 2% to 3%
- **Less than 1%**
- 5% to 7%
- 10%

*Explanation: This procedure shows very low surgical morbidity (<10%) and mortality (<1%).*

**72. What is the long-term success rate of surgical pseudocyst-jejunostomy?**

- 60%
- 75%
- **Approximately 90%**
- 95%

## Resection Procedures - Pancreaticoduodenectomy

**73. Who first described total pancreatoduodenectomy for pain relief in chronic pancreatitis?**

- Beger
- Frey
- **Allan Whipple**
- Partington

*Explanation: Historical approaches in CP surgery included total pancreatoduodenectomy for pain relief as described by Allan Whipple in the 1940s.*

**74. What is the most common procedure for chronic pancreatitis patients with inflammatory pancreatic head mass?**

- Distal pancreatectomy
- **Pancreaticoduodenectomy (PD)**
- Total pancreatectomy
- Frey procedure

*Explanation: Later, pancreaticoduodenectomy (PD) has been the most common procedure for CP patients, with the typical finding of an inflammatory pancreatic head mass.*

**75. What is the main disadvantage of pancreaticoduodenectomy in chronic pancreatitis?**

- High mortality rate
- **Relatively great loss of tissue by removal of the entire head**
- Poor pain relief
- High recurrence rate

*Explanation: The potential disadvantages of PD in CP are the relatively great loss of tissue by removal of the entire head.*

**76. What makes pancreaticoduodenectomy technically challenging in chronic pancreatitis?**

- Small pancreatic size
- **Inflammatory changes in the surrounding tissue of the pancreatic head**
- Lack of surgical expertise
- Patient's young age

*Explanation: Especially dissection along the portal vein and tunneling the pancreas before transection of the pancreatic neck is often challenging due to inflammatory changes.*

## Duodenum-Preserving Pancreatic Head Resection (DPPHR)

**77. When was the Beger procedure (original DPPHR) introduced?**

- 1960
- **1972**
- 1980
- 1990

*Explanation: The original method introduced by Beger in 1972 consists of a transection of the pancreas on the porto-mesenteric axis.*

**78. What is the key feature of all DPPHR modifications?**

- Complete removal of the pancreatic head
- **Partial resection of the pancreatic head and preservation of the physiologic gastroduodenal passage**
- Total pancreatectomy with islet autotransplantation
- Resection of the duodenum

*Explanation: The common features of all DPPHR modifications are the partial resection of the pancreatic head and the preservation of the physiologic gastroduodenal passage.*

**79. What is the main difference between the Beger and Frey procedures?**

- Beger removes more tissue
- **Frey has a smaller excavation of the pancreatic head and longitudinal opening of the duct without transecting the pancreatic neck**
- Beger preserves the duodenum, Frey does not
- Frey is only for cancer patients

*Explanation: The Frey modification describes a smaller excavation of the pancreatic head and a longitudinal opening of the main pancreatic duct toward the tail without transecting the pancreatic neck above the portal vein.*

**80. When was the Frey modification introduced?**

- 1970s
- **1980s**
- 1990s
- 2000s

*Explanation: The Frey modification of DPPHR has been introduced in the 1980s.*

**81. When was the Berne modification introduced?**

- 1970s
- 1980s
- **Late 1990s**
- 2010s

*Explanation: The third type of DPPHR is the Berne modification, which was introduced in the late 1990s.*

**82. What is the main advantage of the Berne modification over the Beger procedure?**

- More tissue is removed
- **Technically easier because preparation of the portal vein is not required**
- Better long-term pain relief
- Lower cost

*Explanation: This procedure offers the advantage of a tissue-sparing resection and is often technically easier to perform than PD or the Beger procedure because the preparation of the portal vein and tunneling of the pancreas is not required.*

**83. What is the surgical morbidity rate for DPPHR and PD procedures?**

- 5% to 8%
- **10% to 15%**
- 20% to 25%
- 30% to 35%

*Explanation: Basically, all DPPHR and PD procedures are comparable with respect to surgical morbidity and mortality, which is low (10%–15% and 0%–2%, respectively).*

**84. What is the mortality rate for DPPHR and PD procedures?**

- 0%
- **0% to 2%**
- 3% to 5%
- 5% to 10%

*Explanation: Basically, all DPPHR and PD procedures are comparable with respect to surgical morbidity and mortality, which is low (10%–15% and 0%–2%, respectively).*

**85. What percentage of patients are pain-free after DPPHR or PD?**

- 40% to 50%
- 55% to 65%
- **70% to 90%**
- 95% to 100%

*Explanation: A high level of pain control is achieved, with a 70% to 90% proportion of patients who are pain-free.*

**86. What percentage of patients show major improvement in quality of life after DPPHR or PD?**

- 50%
- 65%
- **Up to 80%**
- 90%

*Explanation: A major improvement in quality of life in up to 80% is achieved.*

**87. What percentage of patients achieve occupational rehabilitation after DPPHR or PD?**

- 40% to 50%
- 55% to 65%
- **70% to 80%**
- 85% to 90%

*Explanation: This is associated with occupational rehabilitation in 70% to 80% of patients.*

**88. How many patients were included in the CHROPAC RCT comparing DPPHR and PD?**

- 100
- 150
- **226**
- 300

*Explanation: Including a total number of 226 patients (DPPHR n = 115, PD n = 111), quality of life after 24 months was analyzed.*

**89. What was the only surgical parameter significantly different between DPPHR and PD in the CHROPAC trial?**

- Blood loss
- Need for transfusion
- **Operation time**
- Length of hospital stay

*Explanation: Operation time was the only surgical parameter that was significantly different (DPPHR < PD), whereas all short-term outcomes were similar in both groups.*

**90. What percentage of DPPHR patients underwent rehospitalization for CP-associated problems compared to PD patients after 24 months?**

- 15% DPPHR vs. 10% PD
- 20% DPPHR vs. 15% PD
- **27% DPPHR vs. 11% PD**
- 35% DPPHR vs. 20% PD

*Explanation: After 24 months, DPPHR patients underwent rehospitalization for CP-associated problems significantly more often (27% vs. 11%).*

**91. What percentage of patients in the CHROPAC trial had portal venous hypertension making PD technically impossible?**

- 5%
- **12%**
- 20%
- 30%

*Explanation: DPPHR represents an alternative procedure especially important in CP patients who show portal venous hypertension, which was observed in 12% of all patients included in the CHROPAC trial.*

**92. What is the most important postoperative complication after distal pancreatectomy?**

- Bleeding
- Infection
- **Pancreatic fistula**
- Bile leak

- 10%
- 20%
- **Approximately 30%**
- 50%

- 15%
- 25%
- **40%**
- 60%

**95. What is the maximum recommended percentage of pancreatic tissue that should be resected during distal pancreatectomy?**

- 20% to 30%
- **40% to 50%**

- 80% to 90%

## Total Pancreatectomy with Islet Autotransplantation (TPIAT)

**96. When was total pancreatectomy with islet autotransplantation first reported?**

- 1968
- **1978**
- 1988
- 1998

*Explanation: Total pancreatectomy with islet autotransplantation (TPIAT) was reported in 1978.*

**97. What is the main concept behind TPIAT?**

- To preserve pancreatic function completely
- **Complete removal of pancreas for pain relief while avoiding brittle diabetes through islet autotransplantation**
- To avoid surgery entirely
- To treat pancreatic cancer

*Explanation: The concept is that complete removal of the pancreas leads to complete relief of intractable pain in CP and islet cell autotransplantation can avoid brittle DM.*

**98. What percentage of children achieve complete pain relief after TPIAT?**

- 70% to 80%
- 85% to 90%
- **95% to 100%**
- 100%

*Explanation: Especially in children, complete pain relief is reported in 95% to 100% of cases.*

**99. What percentage of adult patients achieve pain relief with opioid independency after TPIAT in the long-term?**

- 20% to 30%
- **Approximately 50%**
- 70% to 80%
- 90%

*Explanation: In adult patients, pain relief with opioid independency is achieved in approximately 50% in the long-term course.*

**100. What percentage of patients achieve complete insulin independency after TPIAT?**

- 5% to 10%
- **One third**
- 50%
- 70%

*Explanation: After TPIAT, complete insulin independency is achieved in only one third of patients.*

**101. What percentage of patients show overall improvement in quality of life after TPIAT at 2 years?**

- 70%
- 80%
- **90%**
- 95%

*Explanation: Outcomes of TPIAT show an overall improvement in quality of life in 90% of patients after 2 years.*

**102. What percentage of patients show overall improvement in quality of life after TPIAT at 5 years?**

- 70%
- **85%**
- 90%
- 95%

*Explanation: Outcomes show 85% improvement in quality of life after 5 years.*

**103. Which type of chronic pancreatitis results in worse outcomes after TPIAT?**

- Hereditary CP
- Idiopathic CP
- **Alcoholic CP**
- Autoimmune pancreatitis

*Explanation: Pain relief depends on the underlying etiology of CP, with alcoholic CP resulting in worse outcomes than CP of other causes.*

**104. What is a contraindication for TPIAT in adults with chronic pancreatitis?**

- Young age
- **End-stage disease with exocrine and complete endocrine failure**
- Recent onset of disease
- Mild pain only

*Explanation: Adults with CP who have end-stage disease with exocrine and complete endocrine failure are not suitable for TPIAT if there are few or no functioning islets present.*

- **No**
- Yes, several

## General Questions on Management

**107. What are the major aims of therapy in chronic pancreatitis?**

- Cure the disease completely
- **Prevention of acute pain attacks, long-lasting pain relief, prevention of disease progression, correction of metabolic consequences**
- Surgical removal of the entire pancreas only
- Long-term opioid use

*Explanation: The major aims of therapy in CP are prevention of acute pain attacks, long-lasting pain relief, prevention of disease progression, correction of metabolic consequences, and restoration of a good quality of life.*

**108. What interdisciplinary expertise is required for chronic pancreatitis management?**

- Surgery only
- Gastroenterology only

- Radiology only

**109. What is the typical median survival time used for calculating prevalence of chronic pancreatitis?**

- 10 years
- **20 years**
- 30 years
- 40 years

**110. What is the characteristic imaging finding of autoimmune pancreatitis in only 50% of patients?**

- Atrophic pancreas

- 6 months

- **46% to 76%**

- **14%**

- **49% to 51%**

- Only adult patients

**146. What percentage of patients achieve pain control or complete absence of pain as the major aim of CP therapy?**

- 60%

- Distal pancreatectomy with splenectomy

**148. What is the main advantage of resection over drainage alone in chronic pancreatitis surgery?**

**149. What is the recommended approach for standard resections in chronic pancreatitis?**

- Only robotic surgery
